title: Word Formation — Advanced
description: Master advanced word formation for Grade 11: Latin/Greek prefixes and suffixes, derivational morphology, compounding and conversion (zero derivation) — bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Latin/Greek Affixes & Derivational Suffixes
topics.concept:
Prefixes (mostly Latin/Greek) change meaning:

PrefixMeaningExample
anti-againstantiseptic
circum-aroundcircumnavigate
inter-betweeninternational
sub-undersubmarine
super-/hyper-above/oversupersonic, hyperactive
mono-/multi-one/manymonologue, multimedia

Derivational suffixes change the part of speech:

  • Noun: -ance/-ence, -tion/-sion, -ism, -ity, -ship, -hood
  • Adjective: -ive, -ous, -ful, -less, -able/-ible, -al, -ic
  • Verb: -ize/-ise, -ify, -en
  • Adverb: -ly, -ward(s), -wise

So 'globe' → 'global' (adj) → 'globalise' (verb) → 'globalisation' (noun).

topics.title: Compounding & Conversion (Zero Derivation)
topics.concept:
Compounding joins two words into one:

  • Compound nouns: bookstore, sunrise, heartbeat, mother-in-law.
  • Compound adjectives: well-known, hard-working, long-term, ten-year-old.
  • Hyphenation: compound adjectives before a noun usually take a hyphen (a well-known author), but not after a verb (the author is well known).

Conversion (zero derivation) changes a word's part of speech without adding an affix:

FromToExample
noun → verbwater → to waterWater the plants.
verb → nounrun → a runGo for a run.
adjective → verbclean → to cleanClean the room.

Conversion is everywhere in modern English ('to google', 'to friend') — the same form, a new job.

examples.problem: Compound adjective: 'a man who works hard' = a ___ man.
examples.solution: a hard-working man — hyphenated compound adjective before the noun.
They milk the cows at dawn. — noun 'milk' converted to a verb.

recap: Compound adjectives before a noun take a hyphen (well-known author)
Conversion changes part of speech with no affix (water → to water)

options: The author is well-known. The event was well organised.

intro.en: English builds its huge vocabulary from a small toolkit of roots, prefixes and suffixes — many from Latin and Greek. Once you know the parts, you can both build precise words and decode unfamiliar ones. 'Transcontinental' = trans (across) + continent + al; 'biography' = bio (life) + graph (write). Word formation turns guessing into knowing.
intro.hi: अंग्रेज़ी अपनी विशाल शब्द-सम्पदा को मूल, उपसर्ग और प्रत्यय के छोटे टूलकिट से बनाती है — जिनमें से कई लैटिन और ग्रीक से हैं। भागों को जान लेने पर आप सटीक शब्द बना भी सकते हैं और अपरिचित शब्दों को समझ भी सकते हैं। 'Transcontinental' = trans (पार) + continent + al; 'biography' = bio (जीवन) + graph (लिखना)। शब्द-निर्माण अनुमान को ज्ञान में बदल देता है।

real_life.situation:
You meet a new word and decode it:

Word: 'incomprehensible'

Decode: in- (not) + com- (together) + prehend (grasp) + -ible (able to) = 'not able to be grasped/understood'.
real_life.why: You did not need a dictionary — the parts told you the meaning. That is the power of advanced word formation: it lets you read and write with confidence even when the exact word is new to you.

rule_box.example: anti + bio + tic = antibiotic (against + life + adjective/noun)

common_mistakes.note: Hyphenate a compound adjective before a noun.

reading.passage: The microbiologist's discovery was revolutionary. By combining 'micro' (small), 'bio' (life) and '-logy' (study), the word itself describes her field. Her hyperactive curiosity and well-trained eye led to a state-of-the-art technique. Soon, hospitals began to 'fast-track' the test — a noun turned into a verb. International journals praised her, and the once-unpronounceable term became everyday vocabulary.

questions.q: Break 'microbiologist' into its parts and meanings.
questions.answer: micro (small) + bio (life) + log(y) (study of) + -ist (person) = one who studies small life forms.
